usage: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅏ
개 is the all-purpose counter for items
compound: noun + noun, no particle between them
examples: 바나나 주세요.
A banana, please.
bare noun + 주세요 is the simplest way to ask for something
저는 아침마다 바나나를 먹어요.
I eat a banana every morning.
마다 means 'every'; 를 marks the thing eaten
바나나가 너무 익어서 갈색이 됐어요.
The banana got too ripe so it turned brown.
real kitchen complaint; -아서 links cause to result
nuance: 바나나 is a loanword (from English 'banana') written in Hangul, and unlike English it carries no plural form — one banana and a whole bunch are both just 바나나, with quantity shown by a number plus the counter 개 (바나나 세 개). Koreans give every syllable equal length and a flat, even rhythm (ba-na-na), without the stressed first syllable English speakers instinctively add. Note the spelling difference: the fruit is 바나나, but a near-look-alike loanword 바나 does not exist, so don't shorten it. It pairs naturally with 익다 (to ripen), 까다 (to peel), and the compound 바나나 우유 (the beloved banana-flavored milk). The classic English-speaker trap is adding an English-style plural ('바나나들' for 'bananas') — 들 is grammatically possible but sounds unnatural for fruit you'd buy or eat, so leave the noun bare and let context or a counter carry the number.

mistakes: Saying '바나나들을 먹어요' to mean 'I eat bananas' — Korean does not pluralize food nouns this way; 들 sounds forced. Use the bare noun: 바나나를 먹어요.
Stressing the first syllable like English BA-nana. Korean has no word stress; pronounce all three syllables evenly or you sound unnatural.
Writing the subject as '바나나는' when first introducing it in a sentence like 'the banana is yellow' — for a plain new fact use 바나나가 노래요; 는 adds a contrast nuance you may not intend.

usage: object marker 를 after the vowel 이
examples: 딸기 좋아해요?
Do you like strawberries?
drop the particle in casual speech: 딸기(를) 좋아해요
이 딸기가 정말 달고 맛있어요.
These strawberries are really sweet and tasty.
달다 + 맛있다 linked with 고; 가 marks the topic being judged
봄에 딸기가 제철이라 가격이 싸요.
Strawberries are in season in spring so they're cheap.
제철 = peak season; -이라(서) gives the reason
nuance: 딸기 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean and not a loanword), so it never takes a plural ending — a single berry and a whole carton are both 딸기. It is strongly tied to spring (봄), the season when it is 제철 (at its peak), and it is the default 'pink/sweet' flavor in Korea: 딸기 우유, 딸기 아이스크림, 딸기 케이크 all mean the flavor, with no actual berries guaranteed. Don't confuse 딸기 with 산딸기 — 산딸기 (literally 'mountain strawberry') is a wild raspberry, a different fruit. The English-speaker pitfall here is double: first, pluralizing ('딸기들') which sounds unnatural for fruit; second, mishearing the tense double consonant ㄸ at the start — it is a hard, unaspirated 'tt', not a soft English 'd', so 딸기 (ttalgi) is not 달기. It collocates with 달다 (sweet), 빨갛다 (red), 따다 (to pick), and 씻다 (to wash).

mistakes: Pronouncing 딸기 with a soft English 'd' (dalgi). The initial ㄸ is a tense consonant; say a tight, unaspirated 'tt' or the word sounds like a different one.
Using 딸기들 for 'strawberries'. Korean fruit nouns stay bare; the plural marker 들 is unnatural here. Say 딸기를 먹어요 for any amount.
Calling a raspberry 딸기. A wild raspberry is 산딸기 and a regular one is 라즈베리 — 딸기 alone always means the cultivated strawberry.

usage: object marker 를 after the vowel ㅗ
달다 → 달아요; 가 marks the subject
examples: 포도 한 송이 주세요.
One bunch of grapes, please.
송이 is the natural counter, not 개
이 포도가 씨가 없어서 먹기 편해요.
These grapes are seedless so they're easy to eat.
씨 = seed; -아서 gives the reason, 먹기 편하다 = easy to eat
가을이 되면 포도가 정말 달아져요.
When autumn comes, grapes get really sweet.
-아지다 shows a change of state (become sweet)
nuance: 포도 is Sino-Korean, written 葡萄 (the two characters together simply name the fruit; neither is used alone in everyday Korean). It is grammatically a mass/group word, so it is never pluralized and a 'bunch' is counted with the counter 송이 (포도 한 송이), the same counter used for a cluster of flowers — using the all-purpose 개 here sounds childish or wrong. A single grape, if you must, is 포도 한 알 (알 = a small round unit, like a bead or pellet). Like 딸기, it doubles as a flavor word: 포도 주스, 포도 사탕, 포도 맛 candy. The English-speaker trap is treating 'grapes' as inherently plural and reaching for a plural marker, or saying 포도 한 개 — instead, learn the pair 송이 (bunch) and 알 (single grape). It collocates with 달다 (sweet), 시다 (sour), 씨 (seed/pip), and 따다 (to pick).

Adding a plural like 포도들 because English 'grapes' is plural. 포도 is already a group noun — keep it bare.
Mixing up 송이 and 알: 송이 = a whole bunch, 알 = one individual grape. Asking for 포도 한 송이 at a store gets you a full bunch, not one grape.

usage: object marker 을 after the consonant ㄱ (받침)
크다 → 커요 (ㅡ drop); 이 after 받침
examples: 수박 한 통 주세요.
One whole watermelon, please.
ask for a whole one with 통, not 개
여름에는 수박을 차갑게 해서 먹어요.
In summer we chill the watermelon and eat it.
차갑게 하다 = make cold; -아서 links the two actions
수박이 잘 익었는지 두드려 봐요.
Tap it to see if the watermelon is ripe.
익다 = ripen; -는지 봐요 = check whether
nuance: 수박 is a native Korean word and the icon of Korean summer (여름) — eaten ice-cold in thick slices to beat the heat, often after a meal. The crucial point is counting: a whole melon is 수박 한 통 (통 is the counter for large hollow/rounded items, also used for buckets), while a cut wedge is 수박 한 조각 (조각 = piece). Using 개 for a whole watermelon sounds off; reserve 개 for smaller, ordinary objects. Don't confuse 수박 with 참외 — 참외 is the yellow Korean melon, a completely different summer fruit. The first character looks like 수(水, water) by coincidence of sound, but 수박 is native, not Sino-Korean, so don't over-analyze it. The English-speaker pitfall is the counter (defaulting to 개) and the 받침 particle choice: because 수박 ends in a consonant, the object marker is 을 (수박을) and the subject marker is 이 (수박이), not 를/가. It collocates with 익다 (ripen), 자르다 (to cut), 시원하다 (refreshing), and 통째로 (whole).

usage: object marker 을 after the 받침 ㄹ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
개 is the everyday counter for tangerines
examples: 귤 다섯 개 주세요.
Five tangerines, please.
개 counts them; number goes before the counter
겨울에 따뜻한 방에서 귤을 까 먹어요.
In winter we peel and eat tangerines in a warm room.
까 먹다 = peel-and-eat, a fixed cozy collocation
귤이 너무 시면 아직 덜 익은 거예요.
If the tangerine is too sour, it's not ripe yet.
시다 = sour; 덜 익다 = under-ripe
nuance: 귤 is the small, loose-skinned citrus you peel by hand — closest to an English 'mandarin' or 'tangerine,' NOT an orange. The synonym line matters: 오렌지 (loanword 'orange') is the bigger, thick-skinned fruit you cut or juice, while 귤 is small and peels easily; calling a 귤 an 오렌지 marks you as a beginner. 귤 is deeply seasonal — winter (겨울), especially Jeju (제주) tangerines — and culturally tied to the image of lounging on a warm 온돌 floor peeling them one after another, captured in the verb phrase 까 먹다 (peel and eat). It is a single syllable ending in ㄹ, so the object particle is 을 (귤을) and subject is 이 (귤이). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: mapping it to 'orange' (use 오렌지 for that), and pronouncing the ㄹ-final syllable — say 'gyul' as one tight syllable, not 'gyu-eul.' It collocates with 까다 (peel), 달다/시다 (sweet/sour), and 한 박스 (a box of them, the way they're sold in winter).

Pronouncing 귤 as two syllables 'gyu-eul.' It is one syllable, gyul, with ㄹ as the final 받침.

usage: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅗ
examples: 방울토마토 한 팩 주세요.
One pack of cherry tomatoes, please.
방울토마토 = cherry tomato; 팩 = pack
저는 토마토를 과일처럼 그냥 먹어요.
I just eat tomatoes like fruit.
과일처럼 = like fruit; 그냥 = just/plain
토마토가 잘 익어서 색이 빨개요.
The tomato is nicely ripe so its color is red.
익다 = ripen; -아서 gives the reason
nuance: 토마토 is a loanword (from 'tomato') written so that it reads the same forward and backward in Hangul — a fun fact Koreans themselves point out. Culturally, Korea treats the tomato more as a fruit (과일) than a cooked vegetable: people eat it raw, sometimes with sugar, or drink 토마토 주스, far more than they cook with it. A key sub-word is 방울토마토 (literally 'bell/droplet tomato') for cherry tomatoes, sold by the 팩 (pack). Like all loanwords, give each syllable even weight (to-ma-to) with no English stress on the first. The English-speaker pitfall is, again, the plural — don't say 토마토들; the bare noun covers any quantity. Also resist English word stress (toMAYto). It collocates with 익다 (ripen), 빨갛다 (red), 신선하다 (fresh), and 썰다 (to slice).

Applying English stress (to-MAY-to). Korean is syllable-timed: pronounce to-ma-to evenly and flatly.
Assuming a tomato is grouped with cooking vegetables and looking for a special word — in everyday Korean it's often eaten and spoken of as 과일 (fruit); the cherry kind is 방울토마토.

usage: object marker 을 after the 받침 ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
채 썰다 = cut into thin strips
examples: 당근 두 개 주세요.
Two carrots, please.
개 counts them; the number precedes the counter
저는 당근을 채 썰어서 볶아요.
I julienne the carrot and stir-fry it.
채 썰다 → -아서 → 볶다, a cooking sequence
아이가 당근을 싫어해서 잘게 다져요.
My kid dislikes carrots so I mince them small.
싫어하다 = dislike; 다지다 = mince
nuance: 당근 is a native Korean word for the orange root vegetable, a staple in stir-fries, fried rice, 김밥, and soups — usually 채 썰다 (julienned) or 다지다 (minced) rather than eaten whole. There's a famous double meaning: in casual slang 당근(이지) means 'of course! / obviously!' (a pun, because 당근 sounds like 당연하지), but in any food context it is simply the carrot. Note the spelling 당근 with 받침 ㄴ on both syllables, so the object marker is 을 (당근을) and subject 이 (당근이). The English-speaker pitfall is the plural again (no 당근들) and the slang trap — if a friend says 당근! they mean 'duh, of course,' not the vegetable. It collocates with 썰다/다지다 (cut/mince), 볶다 (stir-fry), 달다 (sweet), and 신선하다 (fresh).

usage: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅏ
examples: 양파 한 개만 주세요.
Just one onion, please.
만 = only/just; softens the request
양파를 썰면 눈물이 나요.
When I cut onions, my eyes water.
-(으)면 = when/if; 눈물이 나다 = tears come
양파를 오래 볶으면 단맛이 나요.
If you stir-fry onion a long time, it gets sweet.
볶다 + -(으)면; 단맛이 나다 = a sweet taste develops
nuance: 양파 is the round bulb onion and is Sino-Korean-plus-native in feel: the prefix 양 (洋, 'Western/foreign') marks it as the 'Western' allium, distinguishing it from native 파 (green onion/scallion). That 양 prefix is the same one in 양배추 (cabbage, 'Western 배추') and 양식 (Western food) — a useful pattern: 양 + X often means the imported version. The vital contrast is 양파 (bulb onion) vs 파 (green onion/scallion): they are different plants used differently, and swapping them in a recipe is a real error. 양파 famously makes your eyes water (눈물이 나다) when cut, and turns sweet (단맛) when slow-cooked. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 양파 vs 파 mix-up, plus assuming 맵다 conjugates regularly — it's ㅂ-irregular, so 'the onion is pungent' is 양파가 매워요, not 맵어요. It collocates with 썰다 (slice), 볶다 (stir-fry), 다지다 (mince), and 까다 (peel).

usage: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅏ
맛있다 → 맛있어요; 가 marks the subject
examples: 감자 세 개 주세요.
Three potatoes, please.
개 counts them; number before counter
저는 감자를 삶아서 으깨요.
I boil the potatoes and mash them.
삶다 → -아서 → 으깨다 (mash)
감자튀김보다 삶은 감자가 더 좋아요.
I prefer boiled potatoes to fries.
A보다 B가 좋다 = prefer B over A; 삶은 = boiled (modifier)
nuance: 감자 is a native Korean word for the starchy potato, boiled (삶다), fried as 감자튀김 (fries), or simmered in stews like 감자탕 and 감자조림. The single most important contrast is 감자 (potato) vs 고구마 (sweet potato): 고구마 is sweeter, often purple-skinned and orange/yellow inside, roasted as 군고구마 in winter — confusing the two is a classic beginner slip, and they are NOT interchangeable in recipes. (Bonus: 고구마 is also slang for a frustrating, 'stuffy' situation, while 감자 has no such meaning.) Note 감자 ends in a vowel, so particles are 감자를 / 감자가. The English-speaker pitfall is the 감자/고구마 mix-up and over-pluralizing — no 감자들; the bare noun is fine. The verb 삶다 looks tricky but conjugates to 삶아요 (boil). It collocates with 삶다 (boil), 튀기다 (fry), 으깨다 (mash), and 깎다 (to peel with a knife).

The single most important contrast is 감자 (potato) vs 고구마 (sweet potato): 고구마 is sweeter, often purple-skinned and orange/yellow inside, roasted as 군고구마 in winter — confusing the two is a classic beginner slip, and they are NOT interchangeable in recipes. (Bonus: 고구마 is also slang for a frustrating, 'stuffy' situation, while 감자 has no such meaning.)

mistakes: Confusing 감자 (potato) with 고구마 (sweet potato). 고구마 is the sweet, orange/purple one; 감자 is the plain starchy potato. Recipes are not interchangeable.
Saying 감자들 for 'potatoes.' Keep it bare: 감자를 사요 works for any quantity.
Using 깎다 vs 까다 for peeling: a potato is peeled with a knife/peeler → 감자를 깎다, whereas soft-skinned fruit like 귤 is 까다 (peel by hand).

usage: object marker 를 after the final vowel 이
I season the cucumber (as a side dish)
examples: 오이 두 개 주세요.
Two cucumbers, please.
개 counts them
오이를 얇게 썰어서 무쳐요.
I slice the cucumber thin and dress it.
얇게 썰다 = slice thin; 무치다 = make into a seasoned side
오이를 싫어하는 사람도 많아요.
Many people dislike cucumbers too.
싫어하다 + 사람 = people who dislike; 도 = also
nuance: 오이 is the crisp, watery cucumber, eaten raw, pickled (오이지), or seasoned as 오이무침 / 오이소박이 (a stuffed cucumber kimchi). Its hallmark adjective is 시원하다 — here meaning 'cool and refreshing' (the same word used for refreshing soup or cold water), not literally 'cold,' which is 차갑다; 오이가 시원하다 captures that fresh, hydrating crunch. Culturally, 오이 is a famous love-it-or-hate-it food: some people are sensitive to its smell, so liking or disliking 오이 is a common conversation topic. It's a two-vowel word (오이) with no 받침, so particles are 오이를 / 오이가, and beginners must say it as two clear syllables 'o-i,' not blurred into one. The English-speaker pitfall is mishandling 시원하다 (assuming it only means temperature-cold) and over-pluralizing (no 오이들). It collocates with 썰다 (slice), 무치다 (season), 아삭하다 (to be crunchy), and 신선하다 (fresh).

usage: object marker 을 after the 받침 ㄹ
examples: 마늘을 조금만 넣어 주세요.
Please add just a little garlic.
조금만 = only a little; 넣다 = put in
한국 음식에는 마늘이 많이 들어가요.
A lot of garlic goes into Korean food.
들어가다 = go in/be included; 가 → here 이 after 받침
마늘을 다져서 기름에 볶아요.
I mince the garlic and stir-fry it in oil.
다지다 → -아서 → 볶다, a base step in Korean cooking
nuance: 마늘 is a native Korean word for garlic, and few foods are more central to Korean cooking — it's the aromatic base (with 양파 and 파) of countless dishes, eaten raw with grilled meat, pickled, or 다지다 (minced) into almost everything. Crucially, a single clove is counted with 쪽 (마늘 한 쪽), while a whole bulb/head is 마늘 한 통 — using 개 for garlic sounds wrong, so learn 쪽 (clove) vs 통 (head). It ends in ㄹ, so particles are 마늘을 / 마늘이, and say it as two clean syllables 'ma-neul.' The English-speaker pitfall is the counter (defaulting to 개 instead of 쪽/통), pronouncing 맵다 regularly (the correct form is 마늘이 매워요, ㅂ-irregular), and over-pluralizing (no 마늘들). It collocates with 다지다 (mince), 까다 (to peel a clove), 넣다 (add), and 빻다 (to crush/pound).

usage: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅜ
I make kimchi with napa cabbage
examples: 배추 한 포기 주세요.
One head of napa cabbage, please.
포기, not 개, for a whole head
이 배추가 아주 싱싱하고 속이 꽉 찼어요.
This napa cabbage is very fresh and tightly packed inside.
속이 차다 = the inside is full/dense (a quality cabbage)
가을에 배추로 김장을 해요.
In autumn we make a big batch of winter kimchi with napa cabbage.
김장 = the annual kimchi-making; 배추로 = using cabbage
nuance: 배추 is a native Korean word for napa (Chinese) cabbage — the tall, pale, leafy head that is THE base of kimchi, not the round Western head cabbage, which is 양배추 (literally 'Western 배추,' with the 양 = 洋 'foreign' prefix seen also in 양파). Keep 배추 (napa) and 양배추 (round green cabbage) distinct: they look and taste different and are used in different dishes. A whole head is counted with the special counter 포기 (배추 한 포기 / 두 포기), the counter for leafy clumped plants — 개 is wrong here. 배추 is bound up with 김장 (the seasonal mass kimchi-making) and the verb 담그다 (to make/ferment kimchi, 김치를 담그다).
